prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the time-reversal-invariant topological insulator, and its first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I keep B016 as my preferred configuration after the full first-round exchange. The scientific case is unchanged and, I think, has not been dented: Kane and Mele (2005) identified a Z2 invariant for time-reversal-symmetric band structures, a new topological class with protected helical edge channels that does not rely on a magnetic field or on a Chern number; Molenkamp's group then observed the predicted quantised edge conductance in HgTe quantum wells in 2007, a measurement that could have failed. The mechanism is identified and understood, it has been confirmed across two and three dimensions and many materials for well over a decade, and it is the standard organising framework of the field. That is the criterion I weigh most: not only that the effect works, but that we know why. The citation I propose is deliberately restricted to the prediction and first observation, which keeps the exact credit on three names whose roles are documented in the primary papers and avoids deciding the harder three-dimensional priority question.
statement.case_against: I do not want to understate the objections, because the first round sharpened them. The 2016 prize (Thouless, Haldane, Kosterlitz) is the closest precedent, and I owe the committee a clear statement of the difference: that prize covered topological phase transitions and Chern-type invariants in the integer quantum Hall lineage with broken time-reversal symmetry, whereas the Z2 class and its realisation in a real material are a separate chain from prediction to observation. A colleague could still reasonably call that a refinement. I also cannot make the credit airtight. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe route that Molenkamp tested, Hasan's work established the three-dimensional topological insulator, and any trio will read as a judgement against living claimants. Finally, B016 has no support in the room beyond my own and a listing by one colleague, so I should ask whether my weighting of understanding over breadth of consequence is idiosyncratic.

responses.point: Ranks B059 first as a clean idea with theory and experiment in close agreement and independent confirmation at the 10^-18 level, and places the lattice clock's distinctness from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes as the real test.
responses.response: I agree with your test and I accept your answer in the clock's favour: a magic-wavelength lattice clock is a distinct idea from the comb readout and single-ion control, and the case is clean and independently reproduced. This is why I now list B059 as my first alternative. I would still ask you to apply the overlap test symmetrically. You answered the 2005 and 2012 overlap for B059 by pointing to a specific, separable concept, and the same argument separates the time-reversal-invariant Z2 class from the 2016 prize, which concerned Chern-type phases. My remaining difference with you is about what the prize is for: a clock is a superb instrument whose uncertainty is understood, whereas B016 is a new class of matter whose existence was predicted and then confirmed.

responses.point: Wants the Katori and Ye boundary and the 2003 to 2006 primary record checked, insists the citation say invention and development, and does not regard the comb prize as unrelated to lattice clocks.
responses.response: Your insistence on the original experiment is the same standard I apply to B016, and it favours my three names: Kane and Mele wrote the founding theory paper and Molenkamp's group did the original measurement. I also share your caution on B059 and would want the Katori and Ye boundary and the Lemonde, Gill and Bloom claims checked against the primary record before a two-name citation is final; that check is cheap and should happen whichever way we vote. Where we differ is that you treat the comb as a reason to doubt distinctness for B059 while accepting 2016 as no obstacle to B034. I think you should be as demanding of the moire case on mechanism as of the clock case on priority.

responses.point: Prefers B034 (twisted bilayer graphene) as a quantitatively predicted and reproduced correlated phase, and argues the prize would honour the phases and not the pairing mechanism, accepting that Cao is outside the credited names.
responses.response: I have thought about your argument that the prize is for the phases and not the mechanism, and it is stronger than I allowed in round 1: Bistritzer and MacDonald's flat-band prediction is the cleanest quantitative prediction on the list, and I keep B034 as an alternative. But the omission of Cao as first experimentalist is not a detail; the experimental discovery in 2018 is half of the credit, and under a three-name cap there is no honest way to include the first author's group without dropping a named person. Sample dependence and the unresolved nature of the correlated insulators also mean the physical picture is still moving. Topological insulators do not have that problem, which is the only reason I put them first.

responses.point: In round 1 argued for Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan on B016, leaving out Mele, and ranks the Higgs discovery first on scale of consequence.
responses.response: We are close on the science and apart on credit. Mele is the co-author of the Kane-Mele Z2 paper; leaving out one of the two authors of the founding theory proposal would be hard to defend, and the two-dimensional realisation by Molenkamp is the experimental half of the same chain. Hasan's three-dimensional ARPES work is important and I would record it as a strong claim, but it extends the idea rather than founding it. On the Higgs, I accept that it is the largest discovery on the list, but you concede that no three-name set is clean, and scale of consequence is not the criterion I can defend if the credit is arbitrary.

responses.point: Ranks B059 first, stresses independent confirmation and surpassing in many laboratories, and asks for a primary-record check of the Hall-lineage and Katori and Ye boundary issues, while noting a Hall-lineage conflict he flags for the committee.
responses.response: Your independent-confirmation point is correct and applies equally to B016, which is why I keep the 2016 question as the main open one. On your disclosure, a year in the Hall laboratory does not seem to me disqualifying for a judgement on the lattice clock, but it is the committee's call and I would record it. Your point that the redefinition of the second is metrological and not a new mechanism is one I share, and I would not count it as evidence of scientific maturity. Maturity of a clock is the reproduced 10^-18 uncertainty, and that holds already.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the Z2 time-reversal-invariant class as distinct from the Chern-type phases honoured in 2016; I am convinced, but I recognise a reasonable member may not be.
Whether Hasan, and the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposal for HgTe, have priority claims that a three-name cap makes impossible to meet fairly.

Whether B059 supporters will resolve the Katori and Ye boundary and the claims of Lemonde, Gill and Bloom against the primary record; if so, B059 is the stronger configuration on attribution than mine.
How much weight the open pairing question in twisted bilayer graphene should carry compared with its rapid experimental influence.
statement.conflict_note: No change. No specific conflict with the shortlisted candidates from my profile; none of my frequent co-authors is a credited name. Goran Johansson and Eva Olsson are in the Gothenburg physics environment (Chalmers) but I have no collaboration with them or with any candidate that requires recusal. I have no tie to the Hall lineage, Katori, Ye, or the topological-insulator groups.
